The claimed cluster-wide invalidations do not occur: model/infinispan/src/main/java/org/keycloak/models/cache/infinispan/CacheManager.java:124 only removes the local entry and bumps its revision, and quarkus/runtime/src/main/resources/cache-ispn.xml:26 configures realms as a local cache. model/infinispan/src/main/java/org/keycloak/models/cache/infinispan/idp/IdentityProviderListQuery.java:43 does copy previous search mappings on a miss, but that does not establish the claimed cluster-wide login-path performance regression.

Concede. CacheManager.java:124 `invalidateObject` only does `cache.remove(id)` + `bumpVersion(id)`, and cache-ispn.xml:26 declares `<local-cache name="realms" simple-cache="true">`, so no cluster-wide invalidation happens. The comment's main harm rests on a false fact. What remains, rebuilding a merged entry once per new org, is a bounded design trade-off that mirrors getByOrganization.

debate.texto: backend.WatchWriteEvents (sql/backend.go:558-567) starts a separate poller and channel for each caller, so search.init's stream (search.go:203) and initWatcher's stream (server.go:755) are independent; the search reader cannot consume the broadcaster's events. Init now also runs inside NewResourceServer (server.go:258) before any Watch subscriber can exist.

The PR starts search watching before initializing the broadcaster (pkg/storage/unified/resource/server.go:303-310; search.go:203-213). Each SQL WatchWriteEvents call starts from the latest database versions, so writes between those subscriptions are excluded from the broadcaster’s stream (pkg/storage/unified/sql/backend.go:558-567). A subsequent Watch requesting an earlier Since cannot recover those events: it only filters the broadcaster stream without fetching historical changes (pkg/storage/unified/resource/server.go:847-867).

Keeping FP hallucination. The comment's mechanism is false: the search reader does not consume the broadcaster's events; each caller gets its own poller and channel (sql/backend.go:558-567 `stream := make(chan *resource.WrittenEvent); go b.poller(ctx, since, stream)`), so search.go:203 and server.go:755 are independent streams. And no Watch subscriber can exist in the window: Init now runs inside NewResourceServer (server.go:258 `err := s.Init(ctx)`) before the server is returned. Events before the broadcaster starts were never replayable to Watch even with the old order (Watch only filters the live broadcaster stream, server.go:847-867), so the reorder creates no new loss for any subscriber.

I retain TP: the streams are independent, but the reorder introduces a gap in replayable events. In both base and head, broadcaster.go caches incoming events with cache.Add and replays them to new subscribers with cache.ReadInto, contradicting the claim that earlier events were never replayable. Previously, initWatcher started before search initialization, allowing intervening writes to reach that cache even without subscribers. Now SQL WatchWriteEvents initializes its cursor from the latest database versions after search initialization, excluding intervening writes from subsequent Watch requests with an earlier Since. Constructor-time initialization therefore does not eliminate the loss; the defect is the later subscription cursor, not competing channel consumers.

I concede the cache point: broadcaster.go:211 replays b.cache (100 items, :169) to new subscribers, so my 'never replayable' was wrong. The label still holds. The comment says events are 'consumed by the search reader but never reach the broadcaster' and proposes a 'single shared event source'. You agree that mechanism is false: each WatchWriteEvents call gets its own channel and poller (sql/backend.go:558-567). Also, no write through this server can land in the window, because NewResourceServer returns only after Init (server.go:258-262) and the per-request Init calls are gone. A client's Since that comes from this server is therefore later than the broadcaster's start. The only remaining case is a write from another replica during search init, replayed later only through a 100-item cache. That is not the defect the comment describes and not one its fix addresses.

I retain TP: independent channels do not prevent the subscription gap, because each SQL WatchWriteEvents call initializes its cursor from the latest database versions. A write from another replica between subscriptions reaches search but is excluded from the broadcaster’s stream and replay cache. Previously, initWatcher ran first, allowing those events to be cached and replayed to subsequent Watch requests with an earlier Since. Constructor-time initialization does not prohibit such requests, and restoring the earlier broadcaster subscription addresses this exact loss without requiring competing channel consumers.

Final: FP hallucination. (1) The comment's stated mechanism is false and both sides agree: events are not 'consumed by the search reader'; each WatchWriteEvents call creates its own cursor, channel and poller (sql/backend.go:558-567 `since, err := b.listLatestRVs(ctx)` ... `go b.poller(ctx, since, stream)`), so the proposed 'single shared event source' fixes nothing. (2) Astra's replacement defect (writes landing between the two subscriptions are absent from the broadcaster cache) is not a regression this PR introduces. In base, Init was lazy: it ran on the first Create/Read/List/Watch request (the removed `if err := s.Init(ctx)` blocks in the server.go diff), so the broadcaster's cursor started at first-request time and every write before that was absent from the cache too. In head, NewResourceServer blocks on Init (server.go:258-262) and initWatcher runs at server.go:308-311 before the server is returned, so the broadcaster starts no later than the first request could ever arrive. Writes from another replica before broadcaster start were outside the cache in base and remain so in head; the window is not new. Rule: a human should decide whether 'events written before the broadcaster subscribes are not replayable' counts as introduced by the reorder; I hold it does not, given base started the broadcaster even later.
